***

A small donkey dwelt inside me. Though I held no faith in magic, the donkey possessed an endearing weakness for it—psychics, illusionists, and arthritics who could foretell the rain. 

That was the year I lost the simple art of walking. I overthought the movement and could no longer catch the rhythm. It was the donkey who re-taught me. “This foot,” it would guide. “Yes, then that one. And swing your arms as though you are entering a courtroom to be exonerated of a crime you most certainly committed.” 

Next came the sleeplessness, born from the constant need to crank the generator inside my chest. Seeing how overworked I was, the donkey finally extracted it—it looked pristine and bright, like a silver dollar—and cast it into a flock of birds embarking on a long journey toward safety. It was then I realized I was a formidable and dangerous man, harboring such a creature within me, yet I felt utterly futile. 

One day, during our final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing. 

“The somber ones,” I replied. 

“Poor kid,” it said softly. 

“Will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?” 

“No. I think I ought to be leaving soon. I should go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river.” 

“Yes,” I answered. “I suppose you have many important matters to attend to. But perhaps, one day, I will join you for a drink or, perhaps, a brief nap.”

During that particular period, my ability to stride failed me because I overanalyzed my movements, ruining my natural cadence. The animal coached me anew, directing my steps sequentially—first one, then the other—and telling me to move my arms forcefully, mimicking a guilty defendant walking into court hoping to be acquitted of a crime he indisputably committed. 

Insomnia struck next, driven by the need to endlessly turn a manual power mechanism situated in my torso. Recognizing my deep fatigue, the burro eventually extracted the device—which appeared as pristine as a gleaming silver coin—and flung it toward a flock of migrating birds setting off on an arduous trek to sanctuary. 

Housing such an internal entity made me recognize my own imposing and hazardous nature, yet an overwhelming sense of powerlessness remained. 

Eventually, while giving me a concluding instruction on respiration, the creature inquired about my denim trousers. I informed him they were my mournful pair, to which he offered a sympathetic, "Unfortunate child."

I asked if he intended to remain for a third year, but he declined, explaining that his departure was imminent so he could anticipate my eventual arrival along the banks of a distorted river. I acknowledged that significant duties likely called him away, adding that perhaps I would eventually track him down so we could share a beverage or indulge in a quick rest.

For two long years, I was never truly alone in my own skin. Deep within me lived a donkey—a quiet, stubborn creature that possessed an unshakeable belief in magic. At the time, I had forgotten the most fundamental things, including how to move through the world. I moved with a heavy, fractured uncertainty, but the donkey took it upon itself to re-teach me the basic rhythm of walking. Hoofbeat by heartbeat, step by step, it paced inside my frame until my feet remembered the simple, steady cadence of progress.

It did not stop at teaching me to walk. For years, I had suffered from a cruel, unrelenting insomnia, driven by an anxious machinery that refused to shut down. One night, weary of the noise, the donkey reached into the center of my chest, grasped the red-hot, overworked generator that kept my mind racing, and unceremoniously yanked it out. It tossed the humming contraption into the dark void, leaving behind a sudden, blissful quiet. For the first time in memory, I slept.

As our time together drew to a close, the donkey offered me one final lesson: the art of breathing. It showed me how to draw air deep into my lungs without holding onto the panic of exhaling. As it guided my ribs, the donkey paused, looking at the inner landscape of my soul. It nudged me with a gentle, profound sympathy, acknowledging the somber, heavy disposition I had carried for so long. It didn't try to cure my sadness; it simply understood it.

Then came the inevitable farewell. The donkey announced that its two years with me were complete. Its work was done, and it was time to move on. It told me it would travel to a far-off, dreamlike place and wait for me beside the banks of a crumpled river. 

I did not plead with it to stay. I felt no panic, only a deep, quiet gratitude for the peace it had restored to my body. I accepted its departure, knowing I could now walk and breathe on my own. But I hold onto a quiet hope for the distant future—that when my own journey finally reaches its end, I will find my way to that crumpled river, sit down beside my old companion, and join it for a cool drink and a long, well-deserved nap.
outputs.L4:
There were weeks when my body felt less like a living mechanism and more like a decaying house. My lungs were lined with wet ash, making every breath a shallow, desperate struggle. My legs belonged to someone else—heavy, leaden pillars that refused the simple command to step forward. At night, sleep was a distant country I was forbidden to enter; my mind whirred with a cold, manic terror that kept my eyes wide and staring into the dark.

I was entirely immobilized by the weight of my own existence until the donkey arrived.

He did not manifest outside of me, but *within*. I felt him first beneath my sternum—a heavy, patient creature with coat the color of rain-washed granite and ears long enough to catch the faint whispers of my panic. He was a beast of burden, born of some primal, surreal instinct, lodging himself right where my spirit had collapsed.

When I tried to walk and my knees buckled under the phantom weight of my anxiety, the donkey intervened. He did not offer grand speeches. Instead, from inside my legs, I felt the rhythmic, slow *clack-clack* of iron-shod hooves. He took over the pacing. *Left. Right. Pause. Breathe.* He forced my limbs into a slow, unyielding cadence. He cared nothing for my rush or my dread; he knew only the road immediately beneath his feet. Step by careful step, his stubborn refusal to stop forced me forward, dragging my paralyzed will along behind him.

His interventions with my breathing were stranger still. On nights when my chest locked tight—a rusty cage refusing to expand—the donkey would turn deliberately inside my lung space. With surreal, gentle precision, he would plant his hind legs against my spine and kick outward. I could hear the echoing *thump* against my ribs, an internal blow that did not break bone, but shattered the invisible bands strangling my lungs. Immediately, my ribcage would expand like barn doors flung open in a gale. Cold, sweet air would rush into the dark places, carrying with it the sudden, phantom scent of dry hay and summer dust. 

When insomnia threatened to unravel my sanity, the donkey stood in the center of my racing mind. He wore heavy leather saddlebags on his flanks. Patiently, he waited as I unburdened myself. I took the jagged thoughts, the churning regret, the terror of tomorrow, and packed them down into his panniers. I loaded him until he was bowed under a weight that should have broken him. But he merely shifted his weight, blew a warm puff of air through his nostrils, and lay down on the floor of my subconscious. With my burdens held safely in his keeping, my mind finally grew quiet, and I sank into deep, dreamless rest.

Day by day, the beast labored within me. He carried what I could not; he breathed when I was empty; he walked when I was undone. Slowly, almost imperceptibly, the tide turned. The ash in my lungs cleared. My legs remembered their own strength. My mind shed its sharp, violent edges. 

One clear morning, I woke to find my breath coming as smooth and effortless as a river. My body felt light, restored, and entirely my own. 

I looked inward for the donkey, and found him standing at the threshold of my chest, looking outward toward a wide, foggy field. The saddlebags were gone, dissolved into nothingness. His work was finished. He turned his head, his dark, glossy eyes meeting mine with a quiet, profound understanding. 

Without a sound, he stepped out of me, his shadow melting into the soft light of the room. I felt no panic at his leaving, only a deep, abiding peace that settled into the marrow of my bones. My body was intact again. I knew the world would eventually grow heavy again, that the road would inevitably turn steep and dark once more. But as I watched the empty space where he had stood, I felt only gratitude. I knew that when the weight of living grew too great for me to bear alone, I would hear the familiar, stubborn clatter of hooves, and he would return.

Stepping off the noisy, rain-slicked city street and moving **inside** the dimly lit parlor felt like crossing an invisible threshold. The room smelled faintly of burned sage and old paper, shrouded in velvet curtains **that** seemed to muffle the sounds of the outside world. 

For centuries, people have turned to **psychics** during moments of profound uncertainty. Skeptics often argue **that** these fortune tellers are merely masters of cold reading—skilled actors who pick up on subtle body language, a tremor in a voice, or a lingering glance. Yet, as the woman across the crystal-topped table shuffled her worn deck of cards, it became clear **that** the allure of the experience goes far deeper than simple parlor tricks.

What people truly seek when they step **inside** such a space is not necessarily a glimpse into tomorrow, but a deeper understanding of today. They long for reassurance **that** their grief has a purpose, **that** their lost loved ones are at peace, or **that** a better path lies just ahead. 

Whether one believes in genuine supernatural abilities or views them as psychological theater, there is an undeniable power in the process. The best **psychics** do not just predict the future; they hold up a mirror to the quiet, hidden fears and hopes **that** live deep **inside** the human heart. In a world driven by cold logic and constant noise, perhaps the real magic is simply finding a quiet room where someone is willing to listen.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal flash fiction piece that begins with the sentence: "Inside me lived a small donkey."
counterfactuals.output:
Inside me lived a small donkey. 

It stood no higher than my sternum, fashioned from wet slate, grey wool, and an ancient, immovable patience. It paced the narrow corridor between my third and fourth ribs, its tiny, dark hooves tapping a slow, rhythmic *clack-clack* against my collarbone whenever I tried to walk too fast. 

It fed entirely on the things I failed to say. Swallowed apologies were its oats; long, bitter silences were its sweet hay. When I swallowed a bite of pride, I could feel the little beast ducking its long ears, chewing thoughtfully in the dark of my stomach. 

One rain-soaked Tuesday, Clara pressed her ear to my shirt. She didn't listen for the wet, valve-slap pulse of a heart. She listened to the donkey. 

"He’s tired today," she whispered, her breath warming the cotton over my sternum. "He's carrying too much of your gravel."

"He’s always tired," I said. My voice sounded raspy, muffled by the layer of straw accumulating in my lungs. 

Clara reached into her coat pocket and pulled out three sugar cubes, yellowed at the edges. She nudged them gently past my lips. I swallowed them whole. I felt the heavy cubes tumble down the dark throat of my interior, landing with a soft thud near the animal's hooves. 

Inside me, the donkey paused. It lowered its heavy head, nudged the sugar with its damp, black muzzle, and crunched. A sudden, warm draft filled my mouth—it tasted of dried clover, copper, and old road dust. 

"Is he happy?" Clara asked.

"He's satisfied," I lied. 

That night, while Clara slept, the donkey grew restless. It did not bray—it was too small for such violence—but it trotted back and forth along the cage of my chest, its coarse tail brushing against the lining of my throat. It wanted to carry something bigger. It wanted the steep, dusty mountain paths it had never seen, the heavy wooden carts full of iron and sun-baked bricks.

I opened my mouth to sigh, and a single grey hair floated out, catching the blue light of the television. 

I closed my eyes and let my lungs expand, opening the doors of my ribcage just a fraction of an inch. Inside the gloom, the small donkey finally lay down, tucking its thin legs beneath its stomach. It closed its dark, liquid eyes and rested its chin on my diaphragm. 

As it went to sleep, I felt myself grow light. My hands lost their anchor; my feet lifted an inch off the mattress. I realized then that I had never been the one holding my life together. I was merely the wooden cart, hollow and squeaking in the wind, being hauled up the mountain by a creature no larger than a loaf of bread.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of magical realism about a man struggling with basic physical functions who receives guidance from a whimsical animal living inside him. Include strange, poetic imagery and a quiet, poignant farewell scene.
counterfactuals.output:
Arthur’s left leg had become a sack of wet flour, and his heart no longer beat so much as it sloshed, like ditch-water carried in an old tin pail. 

Inside him, nestled in the damp attic behind his third rib, lived a creature named Coro. Coro was an ermine the size of a teacup, with fur the color of milk glass and paws tipped in tarnished brass. He wore a thimble on his head to keep the falling salt from his eyes and spoke in a voice that sounded like a cello played underwater.

Every morning was a negotiation of gears and tallow. 

When Arthur tried to drink his tea and felt the liquid catch—a dry, stubborn knot in the dark of his throat—Coro would sigh, put down his tiny wire brush, and scamper up the spiral staircase of Arthur’s spine. 

"Tilt to the sunrise, old man," Coro’s voice would reverberate through Arthur’s jaw bone. "You’re squeezing the hose again. Give the river room."

Arthur would lean three inches to the east, his bones clicking like dry twigs, and the tea would finally plunge down with a heavy, echoey *gulp*. 

Walking was harder. To move the left leg, Coro had to run down to the lumbar region and strike small flint matches against the sciatic nerve. *Spark. Twitch. Step.* Arthur would drag the flour-sack foot across the linoleum. *Spark. Twitch. Step.* 

"You’re heavy today, Arthur," Coro would pant, his brass-topped paws working the bellows of the lungs to draw in a bitter draft of air. "The wind inside you smells like rusted iron. Have you been eating the dark thoughts again?"

"Only a few," Arthur thought back. His thoughts floated through his bloodstream like pale, luminescent jellyfish, and Coro caught them whenever they got tangled in the liver. "The window is cold today, Coro."

"The window is always cold. Lift the chin. The accordion needs air."

They dragged the day forward, inch by inch, pulling the heavy sleigh of Arthur’s body through the afternoon. By dusk, the sun was a bruised plum pressed against the glass, and Arthur lay upon his narrow bed. The simple act of breathing had become a matter of heavy carpentry—hammering wet oak into place with every inhalation, pulling rusty nails with every release.

Inside, Coro stopped working. 

The brass on his little paws had turned green. His milk-glass fur was smudged with soot from the failing hearth of Arthur’s chest. He sat on the still, warm curve of Arthur’s collarbone, his long tail wrapped tightly around his nose.

"The attic is sinking, Arthur," Coro whispered. The sound vibrated softly in the hollow behind Arthur’s ears. "The joists are soft. I can’t sweep the ash out fast enough."

Arthur couldn't move his tongue to speak. It lay in his mouth like a sleeping toad. But his mind was quiet, clear as winter creek water. *I know, little bit. You’ve worked very hard.*

"I’m tired of the matches," Coro admitted, curling his small body tighter. "The sparks hurt my hands now."

*Then let the fire go out,* Arthur thought gently.

Coro stood up. He unbuckled his tiny thimble hat and left it sitting neat and straight on a ledge of bone. He walked up the dark corridor of the throat, his brass toes making a faint, melodic tapping against the lining of Arthur’s throat, like raindrops falling on a tin roof.

He stepped out onto Arthur’s lower lip.

To the room, it looked only as though Arthur had exhaled a small, silvery plume of mist into the twilight. But to Arthur, he felt the sudden, extraordinary lightness of a house stripped of its tenant. 

Coro sat on Arthur’s chest, fully outside for the very first time. He was no larger than a fistful of dandelion down. He looked up at Arthur’s open eyes, which were fixed on the sky, reflecting the first cold star of the evening. 

The ermine leaned forward and pressed his wet, velvet nose against Arthur’s cheek. It left a tiny spot of chill, like a snowflake that refused to melt.

"Thank you for the tea, Arthur," the little beast whispered to the quiet room. 

Coro turned, trotted down the valley of the patchwork quilt, and hopped lightly off the edge of the bed. His brass paws made no sound as he crossed the floorboards and vanished into the long, blue shadows beneath the wardrobe, leaving the house behind him entirely, beautifully still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Channel the absurd, melancholy surrealism of authors like Richard Brautigan or Aimee Bender. Write a story where a narrator's internal animal guide helps them relearn how to walk and sleep before leaving for "the crumpled river."
counterfactuals.output:
On the Tuesday my knees forgot geography, my legs became two long rolls of damp butcher paper. I stood beside the kitchen table for three hours, holding a cold piece of toast, unable to remember which foot was supposed to feel sorry for the floor first.

That was when the badger inside my ribs cleared his throat. 

He was not a grand badger. He was small, about the size of a folded dishcloth, and he smelled faintly of rain and dry cedar shavings. He lived in the hollow place behind my sternum, right where the sad thoughts usually sat around playing cards.

"You’re standing like a broken umbrella," the badger said. His voice sounded like two pebbles being rubbed together in a wool pocket.

"I don't know how to fall forward anymore," I told him. "The kitchen is too far away."

"The kitchen is seven inches from your left big toe," he said, scratching his ear with a tiny, black-clawed paw. "Put the left heel down like you are dropping a heavy letter into a mailbox. Don't worry about the rest of the envelope. Just the heel."

I tried. My left foot fell against the linoleum. It sounded like an old shoe dropping into a dry well.

"Good," the badger muttered. "Now, the right foot is a secret. You must slide it forward so gently that the dust mice think it’s just five o'clock arriving. Do not think about the knee. The knee is a middleman. Nobody likes a middleman."

We worked on this until the light in the window turned the color of an old peach. By dinner, I had walked four feet. My ankles felt like two small sacks of salt, but they belonged to me again.

"Now," the badger said, stretching his back until his spine made the sound of a dry branch snapping. "We have to fix the dark."

Sleeping had been impossible for months. Whenever I laid my head down, my mind turned into a brightly lit bus station full of people who had missed their connections and were shouting about wet umbrellas. My eyelids were two wooden shutters stuck on their hinges, letting in all the grey static of the house.

"Lie down," the badger commanded. "Like an abandoned bicycle in the high grass."

I lay down on the rug. The radiator clicked like a tiny fingernail against glass.

"Unscrew your ears," he whispered, stepping out from behind my ribs and sitting on my collarbone. He was heavier than he looked, like a loaf of rye bread fresh from the oven. "Leave your ears on the rug beside you. They’ve heard enough about Tuesday."

I imagined my ears resting on the rug, hollow and quiet as sea shells.

"Now," he said, pressing his damp nose against my chin, "fold your ribs. Like a paper map of a city you used to live in, but don't care to visit anymore. Crease the north. Crease the south. Let the middle fade out."

I breathed out. My lungs felt flat, dry, and clean.

"Where are you going?" I asked, because I could feel the space behind my sternum growing cold, like a room where a stove had just been turned off.

"To the crumpled river," the badger said. 

He stood up on my chest and licked his front paw. 

"What is the crumpled river?"

"It’s three miles past the place where you lost your blue coat," he said softly. "It’s made of old carbon paper and wet blue silk that someone folded up and threw into the grass. It doesn't run anywhere. It just lies there, looking at the clouds, waiting for things that are done being used."

"Are you done being used?"

"My paws are full of your knees," he said. "And my whiskers are heavy with your eyelids. I have no more room inside me for your walking."

He stepped off my chin and onto the floorboards. He didn't make a sound. He looked back once—his small, dark eyes reflecting the dim yellow bulb from the hallway. He looked like an old photograph of a badger that someone had kept in a wallet for thirty years.

"When you wake up," he said, "lift your left foot first. It likes you better than the right one."

Then he slipped beneath the gap under the back door. 

I lay on the rug for a long time, listening to the house settle. My ears were on the floor, my ribs were folded like an old map, and my heart beat with the slow, heavy rhythm of a quiet pendulum in a house where everyone has finally gone to bed. 

Outside, I knew, the crumpled river was waiting, soft and creased in the dark grass, ready to take him in. I closed my eyes, turned off the bus station, and slept until the morning came to collect the rent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dreamlike story about an odd inner presence that re-teaches a troubled man how to live. Make the tone bittersweet and include a weirdly specific conversation about "somber jeans."
counterfactuals.output:
The thing inside Julian didn’t have a name, but it had the weight of a damp wool coat and the voice of a harp string plucked underwater. It had arrived three Tuesdays ago, slipping into the empty space behind his ribs where his enthusiasm for living used to reside. 

Julian was thirty-four, but he moved like an ancient clock that had lost its pendulum. His apartment smelled of dry toast and forgotten rain. He had given up on the world softly, without a dramatic gesture, simply letting the days wash over him like gray tide.

Then the thing spoke. It didn't speak in his ears; it hummed directly through his breastbone.

*“You are breathing like a man trying not to disturb the furniture,”* the thing murmured on a damp Saturday morning. 

Julian, who was standing in his small, twilight-lit bedroom, paused with his hands hovering over his dresser. "I am just trying to get dressed," he whispered to the empty room.

*“Look at what you have chosen,”* the thing said, a gentle, raspy sensation rolling up Julian’s neck. *“Put those back.”*

Julian looked down at the dark denim folded in his hands. "They’re jeans."

*“They are somber jeans,”* the presence corrected him firmly.

Julian blinked, staring at the pants. "They're just black Levi's."

*“No,”* the voice vibrated in his collarbone. *“Look closer at the weave. Those are jeans designed for a man who has decided that joy is a breach of etiquette. The wash is called 'Grave-Dust Indigo.' They carry the specific, heavy weight of a Tuesday in November that never ended.”*

"Denim doesn't have a mood," Julian said, though his own voice sounded thin, like paper.

*“That denim does,”* the presence insisted. *“They are apologetic. They say, 'Forgive me, floor, for standing on you.' Look at the back pockets. They are stitched two inches too low, deliberately dragging your center of gravity toward the linoleum. If you put those on, you will spend the entire afternoon apologizing to the daylight for taking up space.”*

"I bought them at a mall," Julian muttered, feeling an absurd prickle of tearfulness behind his eyes.

*“And the mall was weeping,”* the thing said softly. *“Reach into the back of the drawer. Behind the wool socks. The ones with the fraying hems.”*

Julian reached. His fingers found an old pair of light blue jeans, soft as flannel, forgotten since a summer three years ago—before his mother died, before the silence in his heart had turned to concrete. 

*“Those,”* the presence purred, vibrating like a cat sleeping on a radiator. *“Those jeans remember sitting on a warm porch. They remember grass stains and cheap beer. They do not apologize to the floor. Put them on.”*

Julian pulled them on. They felt lighter, absurdly so. When he stepped into the light of the window, the blue of the fabric caught the pale sun, and for the first time in months, Julian felt the soles of his feet firmly anchored to the earth.

Over the next few weeks, the presence re-taught him the grammar of existing. It was a bizarre, slow education. 

The presence insisted he chew a slice of orange until his tongue burned with citrus, making him promise to pay attention to the exact second the sweetness yielded to sour. It made him stand on his tiny balcony in the freezing mist, forcing him to press his bare palm against the wet brick until his skin throbbed with cold, reminding him that pain was just proof of a border between himself and the rest of the universe.

*“You have been living like a draft under a door,”* the presence told him one evening while Julian was boiling an egg. *“You must become a solid object again. A solid object leaves a dent when it falls. A solid object takes up warm air.”*

"It hurts," Julian confessed, leaning against the counter. He watched the water bubble, feeling a strange, sharp ache in his throat. The numbness was melting, and the liquid underneath was hot and painful. "Feeling things again... it just makes me miss everything I lost."

*“Yes,”* the presence whispered, its voice sounding unusually tender, humming low in his diaphragm. *“Grief is the price of admission. You tried to stop paying the bill, Julian. But if you don't pay it, they turn off the lights.”*

A tear slipped down Julian’s cheek, hot and sudden. He wiped it away with the sleeve of a bright red sweater the presence had forced him to buy at a thrift store. 

As the days turned into weeks, Julian began to notice a terrible, beautiful paradox: the more he re-learned how to live—the more he laughed at a dog barking at a leaf, or savored the bitterness of dark coffee, or spoke to the woman at the bakery—the fainter the presence inside him became. 

It was dissolving. It was the scaffolding, he realized, and the building was finally beginning to stand on its own.

On a quiet evening in late autumn, Julian sat on his porch. He was wearing the light blue, non-somber jeans. The air smelled of woodsmoke and old leaves. He felt a profound, aching quiet in his chest, but it was no longer an empty quiet. It was full of the day he had just lived.

"Are you still there?" Julian asked softly into the cool twilight.

For a long moment, there was only the sound of the wind through the drying oak trees. Then, a faint, papery warmth stirred behind his sternum—a shadow of the voice that had saved him.

*“I am almost gone,”* it rustled, sounding like autumn leaves blowing across a sidewalk. *“There is no room left for me. You are too full of yourself now.”*

Julian pressed a hand to his chest. He felt a sudden, sharp pang of grief—not for his past, but for this strange, nameless guest who had dragged him back into the light. 

"I don't want you to go," Julian whispered. "Who will tell me which clothes are sad?"

The presence gave a soft, fading vibration, like a brass bell settling into silence after being struck. 

*“You know which ones are sad, Julian. You’ve always known. Just remember...”* The voice was so faint now, like a whisper carried over a great distance. *“...never wear pants that apologize to the floor.”*

Julian waited. He sat on the porch until the stars came out, sharp and cold and brilliant. 

The warmth in his chest did not return. The presence was gone. 

Julian stood up. His knees popped in the quiet air. He looked down at his faded blue jeans, then out at the dark, glowing city stretching before him. He took a deep, heavy breath—filling his lungs completely, occupying every inch of his skin—and walked out into the night, leaving a heavy, beautiful dent in the world with every step.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a flash fiction story about a man who carries a tiny donkey inside his chest. The donkey believes in magic, helps fix the narrator's broken body, and eventually leaves after two years.
counterfactuals.output:
After the windshield shattered and the steering column caved my ribs into a ruined nest, a tiny gray donkey moved into the hollow behind my sternum. 

He was no larger than a teacup, smelling faintly of dry clover and sun-warmed dust. The surgeons, bewildered by my sudden stabilization, called my survival a medical anomaly. They didn't hear the rhythmic *clack-clack-clack* of miniature hooves against my broken chest wall, nor did they see the silver thread he used to stitch my torn aorta.

The donkey didn't understand human anatomy, but he understood magic, which he considered a far more practical science. 

To him, a fractured collarbone was simply a song that had forgotten its rhythm. Every night, while I lay in the sterile dark of the ICU, he would trot around my shattered lungs, braying soft, squeaky lullabies that coaxed the tissue back into alignment. He believed that if you pressed a bruised heart with enough stubborn conviction, it had no choice but to beat again. When my spirits plunged, he would kick fiercely against my spine, forcing a jolt of warm, irrational hope through my bloodstream. 

"You're foolish," I would whisper into my pillow, feeling his long ears twitch beneath my collarbone. "Bones need steel pins and time. Magic isn't real."

In response, he would nudge my left ventricle, sending a wave of golden heat up my throat until I breathed in deep and painless. 

For two years, we shared a ribcage. I learned to live with the gentle thrum of his presence. I felt his tail swish when I drank cold water on hot afternoons. I felt him nap in the warm chamber of my soul whenever I sat in the sun. He ate my grief, chewing through the dark, heavy knots of trauma until my chest felt spacious and light. He patched my body with stubbornness, stitched my skin with sunbeams, and insisted, every single day, that the world was full of quiet wonders waiting to be noticed.

By the seven hundred and thirtieth morning, I woke up feeling an unfamiliar sensation: whole. My chest didn't ache. My breath was deep and effortless. The scars on my skin were merely faint, silver ribbons. 

I sat up in bed and felt a strange, hollow settling near my heart. 

The donkey trotted up my esophagus. I gasped, opening my mouth, and out he stepped onto my bedsheet. He was no bigger than he had ever been, his coat gleaming like river silt, his dark eyes wide and bright. He shook his tiny mane, scattering a faint dusting of dried starlight over my quilt.

He looked up at me, gave a single, soft *ee-aw* that sounded like a crisp autumn wind, and turned toward the open window. 

"Wait," I whispered, reaching out a hand. "Where are you going?"

He paused on the windowsill, looking back over his shoulder. He didn't speak—donkeys don't need to—but I felt his parting thought echo in the clean, mend space behind my ribs: *There are other broken things.*

Then he leaped out into the morning, disappearing into the golden light, leaving me with a heavy breath, a whole heart, and a world I suddenly believed in.
